key_insight: Diagnostic accuracy alone missed important differences between large language models in psychiatry; clinician-rated reasoning quality separated models that looked equally accurate.
clinical_relevance: If LLMs are used to support clinical decision-making, evaluation should assess not just whether they are right, but how well they reason and explain their answers.
method: Four frontier LLMs generated ranked top-5 psychiatric differentials for 196 vignettes.
Automated adjudication scored accuracy across all cases; five psychiatrists blindly rated accuracy and reasoning on a 30-vignette subset.
The study compared automated scores, clinician judgments, run-to-run reproducibility, and computable trace features.
evidence_signal: Across 196 vignettes, automated top-5 accuracy ranged from 0.759 to 0.837, while on the 30 clinician-rated cases, accuracy separated no model pair but reasoning separated five.
watch_item: Automated scoring and trace-based proxies may not capture clinically meaningful reasoning, so deployment evaluations should include blinded expert review.
paper_title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinician-rated reasoning quality dissociate in a blinded evaluation of large language models in psychiatry
